A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same occupational gender-bias evaluation framework. All 15 pages of v1 and 16 pages of v2, including equations, tables, figures and appendices, support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original pipeline-validation accuracies and measurements of occupational gender distributions produced by four translation systems, including appendix results.

after.justification: V2 retains the original pipeline evaluation and reports translation results for six systems, plus original stereotype, occupational-extremity and correlation analyses.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix B retain the same LLM occupation extraction, fuzzy matching, ISCO-description embedding checks and gender classification procedure. GRAPE is mathematically the earlier normalized GPD metric; its renaming does not introduce a new algorithm.

E1.justification: V2 substantially expands auxiliary data coverage through a newly reported analysis of over 250,000 WMT/C4 texts and evaluation against Shinar's stereotype ratings for 129 occupations. Labor-data coverage extends from 2013–2022 to 2011–2023. The central 9,805-text English benchmark, five text formats, and French/Greek translation tasks remain.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison expands from four systems to six, adding EuroLLM-1.7B and including both NLLB-600M and NLLB-1.3B alongside M2M100, Google Translate and Claude. This adds another LLM family and an NLLB scale comparison. V1 does not identify its single NLLB checkpoint precisely.

E3.justification: The labor reference changes from secondary EUROSTAT/ELSTAT statistics at two-digit ISCO resolution to EU-LFS microdata at three-digit resolution. New analyses introduce stereotype grouping, variance filtering and comparisons over 59 matched occupational groups. Validation curation changes from reported expert inspection with exclusions to approximately 20% random review with no issues found. V2 also corrects the inconsistent per-format benchmark count from 5,833 to 1,961; the overall sample count stays unchanged. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds corpus-coverage feasibility evidence, extreme-versus-balanced gender-assignment counts, stereotype-group comparisons, stereotype-versus-employment correlations, and cross-language/inter-model analyses (Sections 5.2.1–5.2.4; Appendices E–H). V1's detailed format breakdowns and ranked occupation case tables are removed, although some occupational examples remain in prose.

E5.justification: V2 introduces correlation estimation and reports mean cross-language correlation as 0.757 ± 0.140. This spread describes variation across models, not repeated-run uncertainty. Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests; the dataset-length mean-and-spread tables already existed.

E6.justification: From v1 Table 3 to v2 Table 2, M2M100's reported masculine parity scores change from 0.92/0.97 to 0.94/0.95 for French/Greek, and Claude's from 0.82/0.90 to 0.87/0.92. V2 adds results for additional systems, real-reference scores under revised labor-data settings, and extensive stereotype/extremity/correlation results, while removing earlier format and top-five occupation entries. Pipeline accuracies remain unchanged. These are revised reported bias results, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 removes the unnormalized GPD definition while retaining its normalized formula as GRAPE. V1's mathematically incorrect suggestion that normalized GPD can be much less than -1 is also removed. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: V2 removes v1's categorical introductory claim that existing approaches lack mechanisms for quantifying systemic bias. It acknowledges earlier aggregated evaluations and positions novelty around structured occupational coverage, contextual inputs and comprehensive evaluation. The central pipeline, benchmark and reference-based bias-assessment contributions remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning masculine defaults for neutral occupations, rigid learned associations, shared versus language-specific gender preferences, and why data balancing alone may be insufficient. These extend v1's emphasis on outdated stereotypes and data-collection remedies. It also elaborates the exclusion of neutral outputs and makes their future evaluation an explicit direction; the proposed mechanism explanations remain hypotheses.

D1.justification: V2 supplies Claude's translation prompt, specific NLLB and EuroLLM checkpoint links, validation metadata fields, and stereotype-mapping/filtering instructions. It also adds a promise to release code and data upon publication, rather than documenting an available release. These improve documentation without establishing changes to the retained detection procedure.

R1.justification: Section 2 replaces much of the broad NLP survey with detailed positioning against gENder-IT, MuST-SHE, perturbation-based evaluation and Prates's aggregated template analysis. It also adds substantial coverage of gender-neutral translation research and benchmarks. This revises the relationship to the closest prior work, beyond merely adding citations.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and methodological explanations are extensively rewritten. ISCO background moves into the introduction, GAMBIT-MT and GRAPE terminology is introduced, Section 5.2 becomes four thematic subsections, and the appendices are reorganized and expanded.

P2.justification: V1's translation example and labor-comparison bar charts disappear; v2's Figures 1–2 are new correlation heatmaps. The main bias table gains parity/real-reference blocks, new analysis tables replace earlier format and occupation-ranking tables, the English length-statistics table moves to Appendix C, and prompts receive boxed formatting.

improvement.justification: V2 provides more specific quantitative support for stereotype alignment and cross-language consistency, improves positioning against prior work, and adds useful reproducibility details while correcting the inconsistent benchmark count. The gains are limited by removal of detailed format and neutral-output breakdowns and by mechanism interpretations that the correlational evidence does not establish. Overall, the evidence supports a limited net improvement.
